name: Tamil
signature: Curvy and loopy with flat top-bars on many letters, repeated arches, and no continuous head-line.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent 'a' (க = ka). A vowel sign replaces that vowel (க + ா → கா = kā). The puḷḷi ் — a DOT above the letter — removes the vowel entirely (க் = k). Unlike Devanagari, Tamil does NOT fuse the bare consonant into a conjunct: the dot stays visible and both letters keep their full shape. (A handful of Sanskrit-borrowed ligatures are the exception — க்ஷ kṣa and ஸ்ரீ śrī.)
notes: Used by Tamil in this curriculum. The inventory below covers the greeting and self-introduction vocabulary of Chapters 1–2 and grows from there; it is deliberately not the full 247-character grid. Stroke orders are the common handwriting convention, not a standard — Tamil is taught with regional and school-to-school variation. IMPORTANT for authors: a `strokeOrder` list names the PARTS of a letter in writing order; it does NOT by itself say where the pen lifts. The same holds for the sources: the numbered hand-movement arrows in Radhakrishnan's Appendix I, the numbered parts of a writing diagram, and the frames of an animated GIF mark movements and changes of direction, and none of them is evidence of a pen lift. Count a lift only on explicit evidence, such as the pen tip jumping in an animation, a second start dot, or a written instruction to lift. Native Tamil writers draw most letters in one continuous stroke: in HP Labs India's online handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 85–99% of the stored prototypes of each base consonant are a single pen-down stroke. All twenty-nine letters in this starter inventory have authored, font-checked pen paths (`DUCTUS` in language-ladder's `strokes.ts`). க, ச, ஞ, ண, த, ந, ர, ழ, ள, ற, and ன are each one continuous stroke: the manual's numbered movements followed in order without lifting, retracing shared ink where the next movement starts elsewhere (each record says where). The independent vowels இ, ஐ, ஒ, and ஓ are one continuous stroke in the same way, and ஊ is two: உ without lifting, one lift, then ள without lifting, as Module 17 builds it. உ, ட, ப, ம, ய, வ, and ல are also each a single unbroken stroke even though their parts have separate names, and ஏ is a single six-movement run through its hooked diagonal foot. ங was reviewed and keeps its one lift: Frame 2 draws its upright as a separate, detached part before the body, and the print face gives that upright an outline of its own, so one stroke would have to reverse the manual's order or run back over the whole body. எ was reviewed and keeps its one lift for the same kind of reason: Frame 5 draws its right upright last, upward from its foot, but the print face gives that upright and its bar an outline of their own and stops the lower foot well short of it, so one stroke would have to reverse the manual's order, or run back round the bowl, up the left side and along the bar and draw the upright downward. The remaining letters still group their numbered movements into pen-down runs, the reading ruled out above, and are due the same review: அ and ஆ have two runs (one lift), and ஷ has four runs (three lifts). Component descriptions name the pieces a learner can see in the vendored Noto Sans Tamil face; several letters share a straight top bar and are best learned as a family (ச/க, ண/ன, ந, ர, ற).
